what: Geneva drive (Maltese cross) clockwork. Motor A turns a crank continuously; a roller on the crank, 40 mm from its axis, enters one of the four open slots of the star wheel, turns it a quarter turn and leaves again. Between engagements the star stands still. An 8-tooth gear on the star shaft drives the dial through 24-tooth gears (1:3 overall), so every quarter turn of the star moves the dial hand 30°: twelve positions per dial turn. Instead of a locking disc, a friction clutch gear on a fixed pin holds the dial during the dwell. The program turns the crank twelve times (4320°) at 30°/s and checks that the dial made one full turn.
try: Open Cadence with its program, press Reset, then Run. The run takes 144 s: twelve crank turns of 12 s each.
Watch one crank turn: the dial should stand still for three quarters of it (about 9 s) and move during one quarter (about 3 s). Note where the roller is when the star starts and stops moving.
Compare the star’s speed during one step: it starts from rest, is fastest halfway, at about 2.4 times the crank speed, and slows to rest as the roller leaves the slot.

Read the variables: crankTurns counts motor turns, dialSweep adds up the measured heading changes of the dial hand, and ticks is that sweep divided by 30°. After 4320° the program expects dialSweep to be 360° ± 3°.
why: For a Geneva wheel with n slots the crank radius must be r = C·sin(180°/n), where C is the distance between crank and wheel axes; then the roller enters and leaves each slot along the slot, so the wheel starts and stops at zero speed. Here n = 4, C ≈ 56.6 mm and r = 40 mm (r/C = 0.707 = sin 45°). The crank is engaged for 180° − 360°/n = 90° of each turn and the wheel turns 360°/n = 90°; the remaining 270° are dwell. During engagement tan β = λ·sin α / (1 − λ·cos α), with λ = r/C and α the crank angle from the line of centres. The peak wheel speed, at α = 0, is λ/(1 − λ) ≈ 2.41 times the crank speed.
matters: Geneva drives turn continuous rotation into precise step-and-stop motion: film projectors, indexing tables in assembly machines, mechanical counters and some clocks. The step size is fixed by the geometry, not by a sensor. A classical Geneva drive also has a locking disc on the crank that holds the wheel during the dwell; this model replaces it with friction from a clutch gear, so the dial is held only while that friction exceeds any disturbance. In a headless run of the Brickwright simulator the star advanced exactly 90.0° per crank turn after a first step of 88.6°, stood still during every dwell, and the dial ended at 359.5°. Within each step the star lagged the ideal Geneva curve by up to 2°. That is a simulation observation; no physical LEGO build has been tested.
question: The crank turns at a steady 30°/s. During one crank turn, for how long does the dial move, and how fast does the star turn at its quickest moment?
answer: The roller drives the star for 90° of crank rotation, which is 3 s; the dial dwells for the other 9 s. The star turns 90° in those 3 s, 30°/s on average, but its peak speed halfway through is about 2.41 × 30 ≈ 72°/s. Through the 1:3 gearing the dial hand moves 30° per step and peaks at about 24°/s.
further: Change n on paper: for 6 slots, r = C·sin 30° = C/2, the crank is engaged for 120°, and the peak ratio λ/(1 − λ) is 1. More slots mean gentler motion, smaller steps and a shorter dwell.
The wheel starts at zero speed but not at zero acceleration: at entry the angular acceleration jumps to a finite value. That jerk is one reason fast indexing machines use cam-driven indexers instead.

The friction clutch slips the whole time the dial moves, so the crank also has to overcome that drag. Too little drag and the dial could coast past its position; too much and the drive stalls. The simulated friction is a model, not a measured LEGO clutch.
Compare Quartermaster, which steps with a contact and a latch, and Clutch Bench, which shows a slipping clutch under load.
formula: λ = r/C = sin(180°/n); n = 4, r = 40 mm (100 LDU), C ≈ 56.6 mm (141.4 LDU). Engagement 180° − 360°/n = 90° of crank, wheel step 360°/n = 90°. tan β = λ·sin α / (1 − λ·cos α) for |α| ≤ 45°; dβ/dα at α = 0 is λ/(1 − λ) ≈ 2.414. Dial = star × 8/24: 30° per crank turn; 12 crank turns (4320°) → 360°.
